feedbackDefaults.empty: Type a line of working first.
feedbackDefaults.fallback: Not quite yet. Check the denominator and the numerators for this step, then try again. You can open a hint for a nudge.
feedbackDefaults.hint: Try dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor. If that factor is 1, the fraction is already simplest.

explain.title: Make the pieces the same size.

cards.heading: Why change anything?
cards.body: Thirds and quarters are different-sized pieces. You can only add the top numbers once both fractions describe the same-sized pieces.

cards.heading: Find a shared denominator
cards.body: Choose a number both denominators divide into. The smallest one is usually easiest. It becomes the denominator for both fractions.

cards.heading: Make equivalent fractions
cards.body: Multiply the top and bottom of each fraction by the same number. The fraction keeps its value while its pieces change size.

cards.heading: Add, then simplify
cards.body: Add the numerators and keep the shared denominator. Reduce the answer if the top and bottom have a common factor.

tutorLines: We need pieces with the same size before we combine them.
Keep the value of each fraction the same as you rename it.
Now add the numerators. The denominator tells us the piece size, so it stays put.

worked.title: Let’s put it together.
worked.intro: Watch how each line sets up the next one. Nothing changes the amount; we are only renaming the pieces.

steps.explanation: Four is the smallest number that both 2 and 4 divide into. We’ll count both fractions in quarters.
To turn halves into quarters, multiply top and bottom by 2. The quarter is already in the right-sized pieces.
Now the pieces match, so add the numerators: 2 + 1 = 3. Keep the denominator 4.
Three and four share no factor greater than 1, so this is the simplest form.

worked.wrapUp: Same-sized pieces first. Add the tops. Keep the bottom. Simplify if you can.

together.title: We’ll do one together.
together.intro: Type one line of working at a time. Use a slash for fractions, like 3/6. Ask for a hint whenever you need one.

steps.prompt: What shared denominator will you use?
steps.helper: Enter the denominator only, for example 6.

mistakes.feedback: Adding 3 and 2 doesn’t make shared-sized pieces. Look for a number both 3 and 2 divide into.
Three works for thirds, but not for halves. Find a number both denominators divide into.

steps.correctFeedback: Yes. Both 3 and 2 divide into 6, so sixths will work.

steps.helper: Type the equivalent fractions with a plus sign, like 2/6 + 3/6.

mistakes.feedback: The denominator changed, so the numerator must change by the same multiplier. What did you multiply each bottom by?
The first fraction is right. To turn 1/2 into sixths, multiply its top and bottom by 3.

steps.correctFeedback: That’s it. One third is two sixths, and one half is three sixths.

steps.prompt: Add the numerators. What is the sum?
steps.helper: Enter the resulting fraction, such as 5/6.

mistakes.feedback: You added the denominators too. Keep the shared denominator 6 and add only 2 + 3.

steps.correctFeedback: Correct. Two sixths plus three sixths is five sixths.

steps.prompt: Write the answer in simplest form.
steps.helper: If it cannot reduce, enter the same fraction again.

equivalent.feedback: That is equal to 5/6, but both numbers can still be divided by 2. Reduce it to simplest form.

steps.correctFeedback: Yes. Five and six have no common factor, so 5/6 is simplest.

together.finish: You lined up the piece sizes, renamed both fractions, and combined them.

independent.title: Your turn. You’ve got this.
independent.intro: Work through each line on your own. The hint button stays here if you want a nudge.

mistakes.feedback: The sum of the denominators is not a shared denominator. Find a number both 4 and 6 divide into.
Six is divisible by 6, but not by 4. Look for a common multiple of both.

steps.correctFeedback: Good choice. Twelfths work for both fourths and sixths.

steps.helper: Type the equivalent fractions with a plus sign.

mistakes.feedback: Changing the denominator changes the size of the pieces. Multiply each numerator by the same number as its denominator.
The first fraction is right. To rename 1/6 in twelfths, multiply its top and bottom by 2.

steps.correctFeedback: Exactly. Three fourths is nine twelfths, and one sixth is two twelfths.

equivalent.feedback: Keep the common denominator 12. Add the numerators 9 + 2.

mistakes.feedback: Keep the common denominator 12. Add the numerators 9 + 2.

steps.correctFeedback: Right. Nine twelfths plus two twelfths is eleven twelfths.

steps.prompt: Give the answer in simplest form.
steps.helper: Check whether the numerator and denominator share a factor.
steps.correctFeedback: That’s the simplest form. Eleven and twelve share no common factor.

independent.finish: You handled every step without a worked solution in front of you.

completion.title: You found common ground.
completion.body: You practised the full method for adding fractions with different denominators.
completion.takeaway: Find a common denominator → make equivalent fractions → add numerators → simplify.
completion.tutorLine: You’ve got a method you can use the next time the denominators don’t match.
